name: Vulnerability Discovery & Disclosure
description: Finding vulnerabilities at scale, CVE/patch analysis, bug bounties, and disclosure processes.

uss.narrative:
The earliest USENIX Security work in this set attacked two persistent hard problems: automatic exploit generation and patch-presence verification. teEther (USENIX 2018) showed that Ethereum smart-contract vulnerabilities could be found and exploited fully automatically from bytecode alone, while FUZE (USENIX 2018) tackled the notoriously manual process of assessing whether a kernel use-after-free bug was actually exploitable. On the defensive side, Precise and Accurate Patch Presence Test for Binaries (USENIX 2018) gave defenders a way to audit binaries for missing patches without source code — a problem that mattered enormously for vendor firmware. Concurrently, the community began systematizing vulnerability knowledge: Understanding the Reproducibility of Crowd-reported Security Vulnerabilities (USENIX 2018) and Towards the Detection of Inconsistencies in Public Security Vulnerability Reports (USENIX 2019) audited the CVE/NVD ecosystem itself and exposed how unreliable public disclosures could be.

A productive second wave through 2020–2021 pushed automated discovery across new surfaces. Fuzzing matured rapidly: GREYONE (USENIX 2020) introduced data-flow-sensitive mutation to break through hard-to-reach paths, FuzzGen (USENIX 2020) automated the creation of library fuzz drivers by mining consumer code, and Montage (USENIX 2020) applied neural language models to guide JavaScript engine fuzzing — one of the first ML-steered fuzzers at USENIX. MVP (USENIX 2020) tackled recurring vulnerabilities by matching code against patch-enhanced signatures. Firmware became a major front: PARTEMU, FIRMSCOPE, and Jetset (USENIX 2020–2021) progressively improved dynamic and static analysis for the deeply embedded software that traditional toolchains could not reach.

The 2022–2023 period broadened scope to multi-language and multi-component software. PolyCruise (USENIX 2022) crossed language boundaries with dynamic information-flow analysis, Mining Node.js Vulnerabilities (USENIX 2022) caught prototype-pollution and command-injection bugs in npm packages via an object dependence graph, and Fuzztruction (USENIX 2023) attacked structured-data parsers by fault-injecting generator programs rather than mutating raw bytes. Graph-based deep learning arrived with VulChecker (USENIX 2023), which localized vulnerable lines in source code rather than just flagging files. V1SCAN (USENIX 2023) addressed the supply-chain dimension by finding 1-day vulnerabilities in reused open-source components at scale.

By 2024–2025, large language models transformed the field again. PentestGPT (USENIX 2024) demonstrated that LLMs could reason across penetration-testing tasks end to end, and Cascade (USENIX 2024) showed CPU silicon itself was fuzzable with intricate program generation. Patch repair closed the loop: Logs In, Patches Out (USENIX 2025) and PATCHAGENT (USENIX 2025) used tree-of-thought LLM reasoning to generate working patches from sanitizer logs and source code alone, completing the arc from discovery to remediation inside a single automated pipeline.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this NDSS collection was already split between two instincts that still define the area: hunt for bugs, and reason about the fixes. On the hunting side, VulDeePecker (NDSS 2018) reframed vulnerability detection as a deep-learning problem, learning patterns from code slices instead of relying on hand-tuned rules, while more targeted efforts like Automated Generation of Event-Oriented Exploits in Android Hybrid Apps (NDSS 2018) went after a specific platform. On the fix side, InstaGuard (NDSS 2018) tackled how to deploy hot-patches quickly, foreshadowing a lasting interest in the patch lifecycle itself.

The real breakthrough was the fuzzing revival of 2019-2020. REDQUEEN (NDSS 2019) used input-to-state correspondence to blow past magic-byte and checksum barriers cheaply, and NAUTILUS (NDSS 2019) and CodeAlchemist (NDSS 2019) pushed grammar- and semantics-aware generation to reach deep bugs in structured targets like JavaScript engines. This momentum moved straight into the kernel and hypervisor with HFL: Hybrid Fuzzing on the Linux Kernel (NDSS 2020) and HYPER-CUBE (NDSS 2020). Alongside the raw discovery, a maturing analysis thread emerged: Precisely Characterizing Security Impact in a Flood of Patches via Symbolic Rule Comparison (NDSS 2020) asked not how to find bugs but which of a flood of silent patches actually matter for security.

Through 2021-2023 the work fanned out across domains and specialized. BaseSpec (NDSS 2021) compared baseband firmware against cellular specs to find bugs fuzzing could not reach, KUBO (NDSS 2021) and Progressive Scrutiny (NDSS 2022) chased undefined-behavior bugs in the churning Linux kernel, and FUZZILLI (NDSS 2023) set a reference point for JIT compiler fuzzing. Meanwhile the web and blockchain got their own tools, from Probe the Proto's million-site prototype-pollution measurement (NDSS 2022) to Smarter Contracts (NDSS 2023), and binary-level reuse detection matured with VulHawk (NDSS 2023). An In-depth Analysis of Duplicated Linux Kernel Bug Reports (NDSS 2022) signaled a new concern: as automated fuzzers like Syzkaller flooded projects with findings, managing the reports became its own problem.

The most recent work has pivoted decisively toward large language models and toward the disclosure and supply-chain end of the pipeline. From Large to Mammoth (NDSS 2025) delivered the first systematic benchmark of LLMs as vulnerability detectors, and the 2026 cohort makes clear where the field now sits: What Do They Fix? (NDSS 2026) uses LLMs to categorize security patches for memory bugs, NEXUS (NDSS 2026) maps CVEs to attack techniques at scale, and Accurate Identification of the Vulnerability-Introducing Commit (NDSS 2026) traces bugs back to their origin commits. A parallel supply-chain wave, including VulSCA (NDSS 2026) for C/C++ and From Noise to Signal (NDSS 2026) for precisely identifying affected npm packages, shows the area's center of gravity shifting from simply finding vulnerabilities to accurately tracking, attributing, and triaging them across sprawling software ecosystems.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this list is squarely about making coverage-guided fuzzing smarter. In 2018 a cluster of IEEE S&P papers attacked the same bottleneck from different angles: Angora: Efficient Fuzzing by Principled Search (S&P 2018) swapped random mutation for a gradient-descent-style search over path constraints, CollAFL: Path Sensitive Fuzzing (S&P 2018) sharpened coverage tracking to cut hash collisions, and T-Fuzz: Fuzzing by Program Transformation (S&P 2018) transformed the target program itself to get past hard checks. Alongside the tooling, the field was already thinking about people and bug classes, with Hackers vs. Testers (S&P 2018) comparing how humans actually find flaws and Precise and Scalable Detection of Double-Fetch Bugs in OS Kernels (S&P 2018) going after one specific, subtle defect.

The next few years broadened the targets and blended techniques. Fuzzing reached into concurrency and systems with Razzer: Finding Kernel Race Bugs through Fuzzing (S&P 2019), into cellular networks with Touching the Untouchables: Dynamic Security Analysis of the LTE Control Plane (S&P 2019), and into firmware and drivers with Karonte (S&P 2020) and the Ex-vivo Android device-driver framework (S&P 2020). Hybrid testing that fuses fuzzing with concolic execution matured through SAVIOR (S&P 2020) and Pangolin (S&P 2020). Crucially, the area also began caring about what happens after a bug is found: Using Safety Properties to Generate Vulnerability Patches (S&P 2019) and SPIDER: Enabling Fast Patch Propagation In Related Software Repositories (S&P 2020) pushed toward the disclosure-and-fix side, a thread that continued with automated smart-contract repair in SGUARD (S&P 2021).

By the early 2020s the work specialized in two directions at once: precision and exploitability. Directed fuzzing got rigorous with BEACON: Directed Grey-Box Fuzzing with Provable Path Pruning (S&P 2022) and later SelectFuzz (S&P 2023) and ODDFuzz (S&P 2023) for Java deserialization, while GREBE (S&P 2022) asked not just whether a Linux kernel bug exists but how exploitable it is. Web and injection scanning advanced through Black Widow (S&P 2021) and Witcher (S&P 2023), and entirely new domains appeared, from satellites in Space Odyssey (S&P 2023) to blockchain consensus in Tyr (S&P 2023). Then large language models arrived: Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models (S&P 2023) tested whether models could fix bugs unaided, and GraphSPD (S&P 2023) brought graph learning to security-patch detection.

The most recent work reflects both a maturing self-awareness and a hard pivot toward LLMs. SoK: Prudent Evaluation Practices for Fuzzing (S&P 2024) audited the field's own measurement habits, while LLMs Cannot Reliably Identify and Reason About Security Vulnerabilities (Yet?) (S&P 2024) delivered a sobering benchmark on where models actually fail. The 2026 cohort runs with LLMs but pairs them with structure and specifications: SpecAuditor (S&P 2026) generates audit specifications to drive LLM bug detection, PortGPT (S&P 2026) automates patch backporting, and SFA-Miner (S&P 2026) plus Contextualizing Sink Knowledge for Java Vulnerability Discovery (S&P 2026) recover richer program semantics for discovery. At the same time the frontier keeps expanding into fresh targets, including zero-knowledge-proof programs in the Language-Agnostic Detection of Computation-Constraint Inconsistencies (S&P 2026), routing infrastructure in The Fault in Our Drafts: Vulnerabilities in RPKI (S&P 2026), browser-extension secrets in KeyChaser (S&P 2026), and even a direct audit of Apple's DifferentialPrivacy.framework (S&P 2026) — showing an area that now spans smarter fuzzers, LLM-assisted detection and repair, and security analysis of ever more specialized systems.

ccs.narrative:
Vulnerability discovery at CCS has evolved from ad-hoc exploit development to systematic measurement and automated exploit generation. Evaluating Fuzz Testing (CCS 2018) was a methodological turning point: by critically examining how fuzzers are compared in the literature, it established standards for reproducible fuzzing research that influenced the field for years. Hawkeye: Towards a Desired Directed Grey-box Fuzzer (CCS 2018) showed directed fuzzing could efficiently reach user-specified vulnerability sites, and Revery: From Proof-of-Concept to Exploitable (CCS 2018) automated the gap between a crashing input and a working exploit.

The 2019-2020 period pushed fuzzers into new domains: Matryoshka: Fuzzing Deeply Nested Branches (CCS 2019) solved the deep-nesting constraint problem through taint-guided mutation, CryptoGuard (CCS 2019) brought static analysis to cryptographic API misuse, and SQUIRREL: Testing Database Management Systems with Language Validity and Coverage Feedback (CCS 2020) fuzzed DBMS parsers using language-aware feedback.

The 2021-2025 era saw LLMs enter vulnerability discovery. Tools like LibAFL: A Framework to Build Modular and Reusable Fuzzers (CCS 2022) provided infrastructure for building custom fuzzing pipelines, while the broader CCS program reflected growing interest in LLM-assisted bug finding and patch analysis, with Locating the Security Patches for Disclosed OSS Vulnerabilities with Vulnerability-Commit Correlation Ranking (CCS 2021) automating patch localization in open-source projects.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list captures the moment coverage-guided fuzzing became the dominant way to find bugs at scale, along with a growing anxiety about whether the field was measuring its own progress honestly. "Evaluating Fuzz Testing" (CCS 2018) called out sloppy experimental practice and set expectations for fair comparison, while a cluster of S&P 2018 papers pushed the technique itself forward: "Angora: Efficient Fuzzing by Principled Search" used gradient-descent-style search over input bytes, "CollAFL: Path Sensitive Fuzzing" fixed coverage hash collisions, and "T-Fuzz: Fuzzing by Program Transformation" rewrote programs to get past hard checks. "Hawkeye: Towards a Desired Directed Grey-box Fuzzer" (CCS 2018) steered fuzzing toward specific targets. Alongside the tooling, the area kept a human and process-oriented track — "Hackers vs. Testers" (S&P 2018) compared how people actually find bugs, "Understanding the Reproducibility of Crowd-reported Security Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2018) probed crowd reports, and "Enter the Hydra" (USENIX 2018) tried to put bug bounties on principled footing — and it began branching into new targets like smart contracts with "teEther" (USENIX 2018) and web apps with "NAVEX" (USENIX 2018).

Across 2019 and 2020 the fuzzing engine matured through a steady stream of smarter feedback signals. "REDQUEEN" (NDSS 2019) exploited input-to-state correspondence to solve magic bytes cheaply, "ProFuzzer" (S&P 2019) probed input types on the fly, and "GREYONE" (USENIX 2020) folded in data-flow sensitivity — all attacking the same problem of getting past input constraints without heavyweight analysis. Grammar- and semantics-aware generators like "NAUTILUS" (NDSS 2019) and "CodeAlchemist" (NDSS 2019) reached deep bugs in structured targets such as JavaScript engines, while hybrid approaches combining fuzzing with symbolic execution appeared in "SAVIOR" (S&P 2020) and "HFL: Hybrid Fuzzing on the Linux Kernel" (NDSS 2020). Fuzzing also spread outward to specialized domains: kernel races in "Razzer" (S&P 2019), database engines in "SQUIRREL" (CCS 2020), library APIs via automatic harness generation in "FuzzGen" (USENIX 2020), and embedded firmware in "Karonte" (S&P 2020). Meanwhile a parallel line focused less on discovery and more on managing what is already known — "Towards the Detection of Inconsistencies in Public Security Vulnerability Reports" (USENIX 2019) audited CVE/NVD data, and "MVP" (USENIX 2020) used patch-derived signatures to catch recurring vulnerabilities.

By the early 2020s the discovery techniques were consolidating — "BEACON" (S&P 2022) gave directed fuzzing provable path pruning, refining the directed idea Hawkeye had introduced years earlier — even as attention began shifting toward large language models. "Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models" (S&P 2023) tested whether code models could fix security bugs, "PentestGPT" (USENIX 2024) harnessed LLMs for automated penetration testing, and the sobering "LLMs Cannot Reliably Identify and Reason About Security Vulnerabilities (Yet?)" (S&P 2024) built benchmarks showing these models still fall short at the core reasoning task.

The most recent work, dominated by NDSS 2026, shows the area's center of gravity moving from raw discovery toward the messy, ecosystem-scale problems of triage, mapping, and supply-chain provenance. Several papers attack the vulnerability lifecycle directly — "Accurate Identification of the Vulnerability-Introducing Commit" traces bugs back to the commit that caused them, "What Do They Fix? LLM-Aided Categorization of Security Patches for Critical Memory Bugs" uses LLMs to make sense of patches, and "NEXUS" maps CVEs to attack techniques. Supply-chain and dependency analysis is a major theme in "VulSCA" for C/C++ and "From Noise to Signal" for identifying affected npm packages, while taint-style detection continues to evolve for modern targets in "TranSPArent" (single-page web apps) and "FirmCross" (C-Lua firmware services), and system-specific hunting persists in work on Kubernetes operators, PLC binaries, and the ESXi VMKernel. Taken together, the trajectory runs from making fuzzers find more bugs faster to making sense of the flood of vulnerabilities the whole ecosystem now produces.
